questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Mutual inductance from a flux linkage
questions.learningObjective: obtain a mutual inductance from a stated flux linkage and primary current
questions.stem: A coil carries a steady current of 4.00 A. Its field threads 200 turns of a second coil, and the total flux linkage of that second coil is 0.050 Wb-turn. What is the mutual inductance of the pair, in henries? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Mutual inductance is the flux linkage developed in the second coil per ampere in the first, M = N2 Phi2 / I1, and the henry is the unit. The linkage is 0.050 Wb-turn at 4.00 A, so M = 0.050 / 4.00 = 0.0125 H. The two-step route agrees: the flux through each turn of the second coil is 0.050 / 200 = 2.5e-4 Wb, and 200 times that divided by the same 4.00 A returns 0.0125 H. As a plausibility check the mutual inductance of any two coils cannot exceed the geometric mean of their self-inductances, and 12.5 mH is an ordinary figure for a pair of coils on a shared iron core. The tempting wrong answer is 0.050 H, which keeps the linkage and forgets to divide by the current that produced it.
questions.hint: Mutual inductance is a flux linkage divided by the current that produced it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: What a mutual inductance actually measures
questions.learningObjective: state that mutual inductance is secondary flux linkage per ampere of primary current
questions.stem: Two coils are wound on the same iron core, and a changing current in the first induces an emf in the second. What does the mutual inductance of the pair measure?

options.text: The flux linkage built in the second coil by each unit of current in the first
The fraction of the first coil's own flux that is wasted around the core
options.misconception: confuses mutual flux with leakage flux, which is the part that misses the second coil

options.text: The emf the second coil raises, without reference to how fast the current moves
options.misconception: quotes the induced emf alone, dropping the rate of change of current that produces it

options.text: The largest current the first coil can supply before the core saturates
options.misconception: confuses the coupling between two windings with the saturation limit of the shared core

questions.explanation: Mutual inductance is defined as the flux linkage developed in the secondary per ampere in the primary, M = N2 Phi2 / I1, so a henry is a weber-turn per ampere. It says nothing about how quickly the current changes; that enters only when the induced emf is formed as e2 = -M dI1/dt, and it is why the same pair of coils gives a large voltage at high frequency and almost nothing from a steady current. It is also not a statement about waste. The part of the primary flux that misses the secondary is leakage flux, counted separately by a leakage coefficient, and 100 per cent of the mutual term can be realised with a well-closed core. Finally, the mutual inductance is fixed by the geometry of the two windings and the material between them, not by how much current the core will carry, which is a separate limit set by the saturation flux density.
questions.hint: Look at the units: a henry is a weber-turn per ampere, so ask what is divided by what.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Peak emf in a coupled secondary
questions.learningObjective: find the peak emf in a coupled coil from the mutual inductance and the current slope
questions.stem: The primary of a coupled pair carries a current of 4.00 sin(2 pi 1000 t) amp, and the mutual inductance is 0.0125 H. What is the peak emf induced in the secondary, in volts? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The emf in the secondary is the mutual inductance times the rate of change of the primary current, e2 = -M dI1/dt. For I1 = 4.00 sin(2 pi 1000 t) the largest slope is 2 pi f Ipk = 2 x pi x 1000 x 4.00 = 2.513e+4 A per second, so the peak emf is 0.0125 x 2.513e+4 = 314.2 V. The flux route returns the same number by a different path: the peak flux per turn is M Ipk / N2 = 0.0125 x 4.00 / 200 = 2.5e-4 Wb, and 200 turns seeing that flux change at 1000 Hz give 200 x 2 pi x 1000 x 2.5e-4 = 314.2 V. Two checks are worth making. The root-mean-square value is 314.2 / 1.414 = 222.1 V, which is what a voltmeter would read, and dropping the 2 pi factor gives 8.79e4, which is the rate of change itself rather than a voltage and is off by a factor of 2 pi.
questions.hint: Find the largest slope of the primary current before multiplying by the mutual inductance.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The ceiling on mutual inductance
questions.learningObjective: state that the mutual inductance cannot exceed the geometric mean of two self-inductances
questions.stem: Two coils of 40 millihenry and 10 millihenry sit on one common core. What is the largest mutual inductance any arrangement of those two windings can have?

options.text: 0.010 H, since the mutual inductance can never exceed the smaller self-inductance
options.misconception: confuses the ceiling with the value, so the mutual term is wrongly capped at the smaller self-inductance

options.text: 0.050 H, since it can be as large as the sum of the two self-inductances
options.misconception: adds the two inductances, a rule that belongs to coils in series and not to coupling

options.text: 0.00040 H, since winding them on one core multiplies the two inductances together
options.misconception: multiplies the two inductances, which has the wrong units for an inductance

options.text: 0.020 H, from the geometric mean of the two self-inductances

questions.explanation: Split each coil's flux into the part shared with the other and the part that stays to itself. Writing the shared flux as an inductance Lm, the leakage inductances L1leak and L2leak give L1 = Lm + L1leak and L2 = Lm + L2leak. Multiplying, L1 L2 = Lm^2 + Lm(L1leak + L2leak) + L1leak L2leak, which is greater than Lm squared for any nonzero leakage. So M = Lm is bounded above by the geometric mean of the two self-inductances. Here that ceiling is sqrt(0.040 x 0.010) = sqrt(4.0e-4) = 0.0200 H, reached only for perfect coupling in which every flux line from one coil threads the other. The sum, 0.050 H, is the inductance of the two coils wired in series, a different quantity, and the product 0.00040 H carries the wrong units for an inductance. Note also that the bound is not the smaller self-inductance: mutual inductance is generally larger than 0.010 H here.
questions.hint: Add the shared and unshared parts of each coil, then multiply the two results.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Mutual inductance from a coupling coefficient
questions.learningObjective: compute a mutual inductance from two self-inductances and a coupling coefficient
questions.stem: Two coils of 40.0 millihenry and 10.0 millihenry are wound on a common core with a coupling coefficient of 0.900. What is their mutual inductance, in millihenry? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The coupling coefficient is the fraction of common flux, so the shared inductance, and hence the mutual inductance, is M = k sqrt(L1 L2). The geometric mean here is sqrt(0.0400 x 0.0100) = sqrt(4.00e-4) = 0.0200 H, and 0.900 of that is 0.0180 H, or 18.0 millihenry. The result passes the ceiling test: it is 90 per cent of the 20.0 millihenry maximum and cannot exceed it, which is what a well-fitted pair of coils on a laminated core achieves in practice. The tempting wrong answer is 22.5 millihenry, which comes from using the arithmetic mean (40.0 + 10.0)/2 = 25.0 instead of the geometric mean; the geometric mean of two unequal numbers is always the smaller, so that substitution always overstates the coupling, and the error grows as the two coils become more unequal.
questions.hint: Take the square root of the product of the two inductances rather than their average.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Diagnosing a mean taken for a geometric mean
questions.learningObjective: identify the wrong mean in a mutual-inductance calculation and give the corrected value
questions.stem: A student computes the mutual inductance of coils of 40.0 and 10.0 millihenry at a coupling coefficient of 0.900 and writes 22.5 millihenry. Which correction applies, and what is the right value?

options.text: 22.5 millihenry is right, since the coupling coefficient multiplies the average inductance
options.misconception: believes the average inductance sets the ceiling, so the coupling is applied to it

options.text: 9.00 millihenry, because the coupling coefficient must multiply the smaller coil only
options.misconception: applies the coupling to one coil alone, treating the mutual term as a share of the smaller coil

options.text: 18.0 millihenry, because the geometric mean 20.0 millihenry is the ceiling, not the average
20.0 millihenry, because the coupling coefficient only marks the direction of the flux
options.misconception: discards the coupling coefficient and quotes the perfect-coupling ceiling as the answer

questions.explanation: The correct route is M = k sqrt(L1 L2) = 0.900 x sqrt(0.0400 x 0.0100) H = 0.900 x 0.0200 = 0.0180 H, which is 18.0 millihenry. The student's 22.5 came from the arithmetic mean, 0.900 x (0.0400 + 0.0100)/2 = 0.0225 H. The two means part company because the geometric mean of two unequal numbers is always the smaller: sqrt(40 x 10) = 20.0 while (40 + 10)/2 = 25.0. Because of that, the average always pushes the answer up, and the error grows as the two coils become more unequal, so a student who gets away with 22.5 here would get it badly wrong on a 400 mH coil coupled to a 4 mH one. The other two proposals fail on a different ground. Multiplying the coupling by the smaller coil alone gives 9.0 millihenry, which would make the answer depend on the 10 mH coil alone and leave the 40 mH coil with no influence at all, and that is impossible since the mutual term is symmetric between the two windings. And 20.0 millihenry is the perfect-coupling ceiling, which a coefficient of 0.900 cannot reach.
questions.hint: Compare the geometric mean with the arithmetic mean of the same two numbers.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Reading a leakage coefficient
questions.learningObjective: identify the leakage coefficient as the fraction of flux that does not link the second coil
questions.stem: A transformer pair has a mutual inductance of 0.0180 H, and it is found that 20 per cent of the primary's own total flux threads only the primary. What does that 20 per cent figure describe?

options.text: The fraction of the input power lost as heat in the primary winding at full load
options.misconception: reads it as a power loss, whereas the figure is a fraction of a flux linkage

options.text: The leakage coefficient, the part of the primary's flux that the secondary never sees
The fraction of the secondary flux that arrives at the terminals a moment later than it left
options.misconception: treats it as a delay, confusing a missing part of the flux with a slow part of it

options.text: The share of the magnetic flux lost as heat inside the core at the working frequency
options.misconception: treats it as a heating fraction, whereas core loss is a separate and smaller quantity

questions.explanation: The flux leaving the primary divides into the part that threads the secondary, which is the mutual flux that produces the useful emf, and the part that goes round the core and back without linking the other winding, which is leakage flux. The leakage coefficient is the second part over the primary's total flux, here 0.20, so only 80 per cent of the primary flux is mutual. That is why a real transformer's mutual inductance falls short of the ceiling set by the two self-inductances, and why each winding's own inductance is larger than the mutual term. The figure is emphatically not a power or a heating fraction: heat in the windings comes from the current against their resistance, and core loss comes from hysteresis and eddy currents, neither of which is measured by this ratio. Nor is it a delay. Leakage flux is absent from the secondary altogether, not late, and a phase shift is a different failure with a different signature.
questions.hint: Ask whether the missing flux is late arriving or simply never reaches the other winding.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Expression and unit of a mutual emf
questions.learningObjective: state the mutual emf expression and check the unit of the henry in it
questions.stem: A primary winding of 0.0125 H shares a core with a second winding. Which expression gives the emf induced in that second winding, and in what unit does it come out?

options.text: M divided by the rate of change of current in the primary, in tesla
options.misconception: divides by the rate of change, so the coupling would weaken as the current speeds up

options.text: M times the current in the primary, in henries per second
options.misconception: uses the current rather than its rate, which describes a steady magnetised state

options.text: M times the rate of change of the secondary current, in webers
options.misconception: applies the mutual inductance to the secondary current and reverses the roles of the windings

options.text: Minus M times the rate of change of the primary current, in volts

questions.explanation: Faraday's law applied to the second winding gives e2 = -N2 dPhi2/dt, and the definition of mutual inductance, M = N2 Phi2 / I1, lets the flux be replaced by the primary current, so e2 = -M dI1/dt. The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced emf drives a current whose own field opposes the change that produced it, which is why the sign appears at all. The units close on their own, since a henry is a volt-second per ampere and dI/dt carries amperes per second, so (V s / A)(A / s) = V. Substituting the numbers, M = 0.0125 H with a primary slope of 2.51e4 A per second gives 314.2 V, the same peak emf the flux route produces, which confirms that the sign is bookkeeping and not a change of size. Dividing by the rate of change, as in the first option, would give webers rather than volts and would also make the emf fall as the current speeds up, which is backwards.
questions.hint: Substitute the definition of mutual inductance into Faraday's law for the second winding.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: What makes two windings couple
questions.learningObjective: identify the shared low-reluctance path as the reason two windings link flux
questions.stem: Two coils of many turns are wound on opposite sides of the same toroidal core. Which single design feature is doing most of the work in making the flux of each one link the other?

options.text: The shared iron path, which carries the flux from one winding round to the other
The number of turns in each coil, which fixes how much flux each one can draw
options.misconception: attributes the coupling to the turn count alone, ignoring whether the flux reaches the other coil

options.text: The wire gauge, which sets how much current the coils can carry without heating
options.misconception: confuses the current-carrying capacity of the wire with its magnetic linkage

options.text: The distance between the coils, which decides how much of the field spans both of them
options.misconception: believes the free-space gap between the coils is what sets the flux linkage

questions.explanation: Mutual flux has to travel along a path. With both windings on one closed iron core, the flux leaving the primary is guided round the toroid and arrives at the secondary, so nearly all of it links the other winding and the coupling coefficient approaches 1. Without a shared path the field of each coil spreads through the surrounding space and only the small part that happens to thread the other coil is mutual, so the coefficient falls far below 1 and the mutual inductance shrinks with it. The turn count is not the active ingredient: it fixes the two self-inductances and so fixes the ceiling sqrt(L1 L2) that the mutual term can reach, but turns alone create no linkage. Wire gauge sets resistance and therefore the heating at a given current, and the spacing between windings matters only in that a wide separation on a large core means less shared path, hence a lower coefficient.
questions.hint: Ask where the flux physically goes between the two windings.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The driving quantity in a magnetic circuit
questions.learningObjective: identify the magnetomotive force as the driving quantity of a magnetic circuit
questions.stem: A magnetic circuit is described in the same style as an electric one, with a driving quantity, an opposition and a flux. Which quantity plays the part of the electromotive force?

options.text: The flux density in the core, since that is what the circuit is meant to deliver
options.misconception: names the output of the circuit as its driving quantity, confusing flux density with mmf

options.text: The permeability of the core, since it is the property that drives the flux round
options.misconception: names a material property as the driving quantity, though the mmf is set by the winding

options.text: The magnetomotive force, which is the ampere-turns supplied by the current and turns
The reluctance, since a larger reluctance is what pushes more flux into the core
options.misconception: names the opposition as the driver, which reverses the roles in the analogy

questions.explanation: Ampere's law taken round the magnetic circuit gives the sum of NI over the path as the field strength H times the path length, and the quantity NI, in ampere-turns, is the magnetomotive force. It is the closest analogue of a voltage: it is supplied by the current and the turns, it is measured in ampere-turns, and it drives a flux against an opposition. The rest of the analogy follows directly, with flux in place of current, reluctance in place of resistance and permeability in place of conductivity, so flux equals magnetomotive force divided by reluctance just as current equals voltage divided by resistance. Two respects in which the analogy misleads are worth flagging. The opposition in a magnetic circuit is usually dominated by a single air gap rather than spread through a linear resistivity, and the relative permeability of iron is thousands of times more than the figure an electric conductor would give, so a magnetic circuit is nearly always limited by one bottleneck.
questions.hint: Compare with Ohm's law and ask which symbol the product of current and turns corresponds to.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Magnetomotive force for a stated flux
questions.learningObjective: compute the magnetomotive force from flux, path length, area and permeability
questions.stem: A ring of soft iron has a mean path length of 0.120 m and a cross-section of 1.00e-3 m^2, with a relative permeability of 1000. Taking mu_0 as 1.3e-6 H per metre, what magnetomotive force in ampere-turns is needed to hold a flux of 0.50 milliweber in it? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Start from the flux density, B = Phi / A = 5.0e-4 / 1.00e-3 = 0.50 T. The material's permeability is mu_r mu_0 = 1000 x 1.3e-6 = 1.3e-3 H per metre, so the field strength required is H = B / mu = 0.50 / 1.3e-3 = 3.85e2 A per metre, and the magnetomotive force is H l = 3.85e2 x 0.120 = 46.2 ampere-turns. The reluctance route agrees exactly: R = l / (mu A) = 0.120 / (1.3e-3 x 1.00e-3) = 9.231e+4 ampere-turns per weber, and Phi R = 5.0e-4 x 9.231e+4 = 46.2. Two checks matter here. A flux density of 0.50 T is comfortably below the saturation value of soft iron, so treating the material as linear was justified; and 4.62e2, the answer obtained by dropping a factor of ten from the permeability, would ask a coil of the same size to saturate the core, so the plausibility of the supply is itself a diagnostic.
questions.hint: Find the flux density first, then the field strength, then multiply by the path length.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Magnetizing current from a magnetic circuit
questions.learningObjective: turn a magnetomotive force into the current needed in a stated number of turns
questions.stem: A ring of soft iron, mean path 0.120 m, cross-section 1.00e-3 m^2 and relative permeability 1000, is wound with 500 turns and must carry 0.50 milliweber. Taking mu_0 as 1.3e-6 H per metre, what current in amperes must the winding carry? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The magnetomotive force is the product of the current and the number of turns, so the current is the magnetomotive force divided by the turns. Working the circuit out first, B = Phi / A = 0.50 T, H = B / (mu_r mu_0) = 0.50 / (1000 x 1.3e-6) = 3.85e2 A per metre, and H l = 3.85e2 x 0.120 = 46.2 ampere-turns, which over 500 turns gives I = 46.2 / 500 = 9.231e-2 A. The cross-check is the scale: for the same flux the reluctance of the ring is 9.231e+4 ampere-turns per weber, so 5.0e-4 Wb needs only tens of ampere-turns, and a fraction of an ampere is what a few hundred turns can supply. A current of 92.3 A, which is what the calculation gives if the core's permeability is left out, would demand 4.6e4 ampere-turns and would drive the iron well past saturation, where no linear answer is valid.
questions.hint: Work out the ampere-turns the flux demands, then divide by the number of turns.

questions.topic: A permeability left out of a core calculation
questions.learningObjective: diagnose the omitted core permeability that inflates a magnetizing current
questions.stem: A ring core of 0.120 m mean path, 1.00e-3 m^2 cross-section and relative permeability 1000 is wound with 500 turns. Someone wants 0.50 milliweber, works out 92.3 A, and finds the supply cannot give it. What is wrong, and what is the right current?

options.text: 0.185 A, because the mean path was taken as twice the length that was stated
options.misconception: doubles the path length, which is the error of measuring to the outside diameter instead

options.text: 0.0923 A, because the permeability of the iron was left out of the calculation
0.923 A, because the permeability was taken a hundred times too small
options.misconception: misses the permeability by a factor of a hundred rather than omitting it entirely

options.text: 0.00923 A, because the permeability was taken a hundred thousand times too large
options.misconception: misses the permeability in the other direction, by a factor of a hundred thousand

questions.explanation: The working is B = 0.50 T, then H = B / (mu_r mu_0) = 0.50 / (1000 x 1.3e-6) = 3.85e2 A per metre, then H l = 46.2 ampere-turns, then I = 46.2 / 500 = 9.23e-2 A. The 92.3 A figure comes from dividing by mu_0 alone, that is from treating the ring as if it were air: 0.50 x 0.120 / (1.3e-6 x 500) = 92.3. That is exactly 1000 times too large, the relative permeability having been dropped, and the thousand-fold gap between the two answers is the fingerprint of the mistake. It also fails a physical check that the correct answer passes: 92.3 A through 500 turns asks for 4.6e4 ampere-turns, which would put the iron deep into saturation, where the linear relation between H and B no longer holds and no constant permeability can rescue the calculation. The other two options are decade slips in the permeability rather than its omission, and would leave the same order-of-magnitude error.
questions.hint: Compare the two currents and see which single factor of a thousand separates them.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why an air gap dominates a magnetic circuit
questions.learningObjective: explain why a short air gap dominates the reluctance of an iron core
questions.stem: An iron core of 0.050 m mean path and relative permeability 1000 is interrupted by a 0.20 mm air gap of area 5.0e-4 m^2. Taking mu_0 as 1.3e-6 H per metre, what fraction of the total reluctance lies in the gap?

options.text: 80 per cent, because the gap's permeability is a thousand times lower over a much shorter length
20 per cent, because the iron is short and so the gap cannot dominate the circuit
options.misconception: reverses the comparison, reading off the iron share and calling it the gap share

options.text: 50 per cent, because the gap and the iron are two equal lengths of the same path
options.misconception: treats the two parts of the path as alike, forgetting that only the gap has air in it

options.text: 0.4 per cent, from the ratio of the gap length to the whole path on its own
options.misconception: uses the length ratio alone and ignores the thousandfold difference in permeability

questions.explanation: The reluctance of each part of a series path is l divided by mu A, and the two parts are in series, so the two reluctances add. For the iron, R = 0.050 / (1000 x 1.3e-6 x 5.0e-4) = 7.692e+4 ampere-turns per weber. For the gap the permeability is mu_0, not 1000 mu_0, so R = 2.0e-4 / (1.3e-6 x 5.0e-4) = 3.077e+5. The gap is one four-thousandth of the path length but the permeability is one thousandth as good, and since the two effects nearly cancel, the gap's share of the total is 3.08e5 / 3.85e5 = 0.800, or 80 per cent. The same figure follows from splitting the magnetomotive force: with the same flux in both parts the mmf fractions equal the reluctance fractions, and 2.0e-4 / (2.0e-4 + 0.050/1000) is again 0.800. This is why motor and relay designers cut gaps in millimetres rather than tens of millimetres.
questions.hint: Add the two reluctances in series, and notice how nearly the length and permeability changes cancel.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Effective permeability of a gapped core
questions.learningObjective: reduce a gapped magnetic path to a single effective relative permeability
questions.stem: A ring core of relative permeability 1000 has a mean iron path of 0.200 m and is cut by an air gap of 0.50 mm. Ignoring fringing, what effective relative permeability does the whole path present, taking mu_0 as 1.3e-6 H per metre? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Reduce the path to one permeability by adding the field-strength drops, because the same flux crosses every part. The total magnetizing field is H_iron plus H_gap, so 1 / mu_eff is (l_iron / l) / mu_r plus l_gap / l. With l = 0.200 m, l_gap = 5.0e-4 m and mu_r = 1000 that is 9.975e-4 + 2.5e-3 = 3.4975e-3, giving mu_eff = 286. Written in the more familiar form mu_eff = mu_r / (1 + l_gap (mu_r - 1) / l) the same number comes out as 1000 / (1 + 2.4975) = 285.9. The plausibility check is the whole point of the figure. A gap of half a millimetre in a 200 mm path is only a quarter of one per cent of the length, yet it cuts the effective permeability to under a third of the material's own, because the gap's contribution enters the reciprocal in proportion to its length and in inverse proportion to a permeability a thousand times smaller. Quoting the material's 1000 would overestimate the core's response by a factor of 3.5.
questions.hint: Add the field-strength drops across the iron and the gap before inverting to a permeability.

options.misconception: ignores the gap area, which enters the gap reluctance as l divided by mu_0 A

options.text: The flux density in the gap rises, since the same flux is squeezed into a smaller area
options.misconception: has the sign of the effect backwards, since the spreading field lowers the gap flux density

options.text: The mmf across the gap falls to zero, since the fringing field carries the flux for nothing
options.misconception: believes a return path of any kind costs no magnetomotive force at all

options.text: The usable area is larger than the metal face, so the effective gap length is shorter

questions.explanation: The field leaving a pole face cannot stop at the face. It spreads outwards near the edges, so a region considerably larger than the geometric area carries flux, and the flux density in the gap is lower than the simple Phi divided by the face area would suggest. Because the reluctance of the gap is l divided by mu_0 A, the enlarged effective area A raises it into the circuit and behaves exactly like a shorter gap. This is why the 0.50 mm gap in the previous calculation is not quite so bad as the arithmetic suggested, and why designers who need a very small effective gap use pole faces with a large ratio of area to separation. The first option misses the point by ignoring the area altogether. The second has the sign of the effect backwards, since the spreading field lowers rather than raises the gap's flux density, and the third is nonsense: a return path of any description still costs magnetomotive force, and fringing spreads the loss rather than removing it.

questions.topic: Statements that hold about a magnetic circuit
questions.learningObjective: select the statements that correctly describe reluctance, permeance and air gaps
questions.stem: Four statements about magnetic circuits are listed below. Which two of them are correct?

options.text: Reluctance is measured in ampere-turns per weber
Permeance is the reciprocal of the reluctance of the same path
A core's reluctance is fixed once its geometry is fixed, since permeability does not enter
options.misconception: believes the permeability drops out of the reluctance, which is l divided by mu A

options.text: A second air gap in the same path adds no reluctance, since flux already crosses the first
options.misconception: believes an air gap adds no reluctance, ignoring that series reluctances add

questions.explanation: The first two follow from the definition. Reluctance is flux per unit magnetomotive force, so it carries ampere-turns per weber, and permeance, being the reciprocal, is the magnetomotive force needed per weber of flux. The third is wrong on the substance: the reluctance of a path is l divided by mu A, so the material's permeability appears in the denominator and a core of fixed geometry can be made more or less reluctant by changing the material. The fourth confuses a series sum with a redundancy. Two gaps along one path are two reluctances in series and they add, which is exactly why several gaps cost more than a single gap of the same total length: the sharing is not free, and a relay with three separate gaps needs more ampere-turns than one with a single gap of equal combined length.

options.misconception: treats the measured mmf of a single limb as the drive around the whole ring

options.text: 8.89e4, from dividing the 32 ampere-turns by the 3.6e-4 Wb the core carries
3.60e-4, which is the flux in webers rather than a reluctance of any kind
options.misconception: reports the flux in the slot where the reluctance belongs, a pure unit confusion

options.text: 2.25e-3, which is the material's absolute permeability rather than a reluctance
options.misconception: quotes an absolute permeability in H per metre where ampere-turns per weber belongs

The independent route through the material's permeability gives the same figure. The measured field strength is 32 / 0.080 = 400 A per metre, the absolute permeability is 0.90 / 400 = 2.25e-3 H per metre, and l divided by mu A is 0.080 / (2.25e-3 x 4.0e-4), which is again 8.89e4. That route also yields the relative permeability, 2.25e-3 / 1.3e-6 = 1.73e3, a sensible figure for a working iron core. The first option halves the answer by treating the 32 ampere-turns as the drive through one limb only, which is the classic error when a ring is measured limb by limb.

questions.topic: Why a keeper demagnetises a magnet
questions.learningObjective: explain that a low-reluctance return path strengthens the demagnetizing field
questions.stem: A bar magnet keeps its magnetization for years in air, but the same magnet laid against a soft iron keeper loses it in days. Which statement explains this?

The keeper's permeability is so high that it steals the magnetization and stores it in itself
options.misconception: thinks the magnetization moves into the keeper, though the flux merely passes through it

options.text: The keeper carries the magnet's flux far away, so the field inside the magnet simply fades
options.misconception: describes a dispersal of the flux rather than a stronger opposing field inside

options.text: The keeper absorbs heat from the magnet and drives its temperature past the Curie point
options.misconception: invents a thermal mechanism, since an iron keeper at room temperature changes no temperature

questions.explanation: A uniformly magnetised body carries a demagnetizing field from its own pole pieces, and the internal field is Br multiplied by one minus the demagnetizing factor, so anything that strengthens that opposing field reduces the internal field and with it the magnetization. A soft iron keeper is a far better return path than air, so it raises the demagnetizing factor and the magnet demagnetizes. The scale of the change is easy to see from the circuit: for 500 ampere-turns and a 1.0 mm return path of area 1.0e-4 m^2, air gives a reluctance of 1.0e-3 / (1.3e-6 x 1.0e-4) = 7.7e6 while iron of relative permeability 1000 over the same geometry gives 7.7e3, so the return flux rises a thousandfold. The flux does not move into the iron, as the second option claims; it passes through and comes back, and the magnetization stays in the magnet. The third confuses a stronger opposition with a dispersal, and the fourth invents a thermal mechanism with no basis.
questions.hint: Ask what a low-reluctance return path does to the field the magnet's own pole pieces produce inside it.

questions.topic: Domains in an unmagnetized ferromagnet
questions.learningObjective: explain that domains in random directions leave a ferromagnet unmagnetized
questions.stem: A piece of soft iron sits well away from any magnet, and a compass needle brought near it shows no deflection. What is the state of the magnetization inside the iron?

options.text: The domains are already lined up, but their fields cancel outside because the piece is neutral
options.misconception: pictures the domains as aligned in the unmagnetized state, which is a contradiction

options.text: The domains point every which way, so their fields largely cancel and little flux leaves
The domains are all aligned along the Earth's field, which is far too weak to attract
options.misconception: blames the Earth's field, which is present before the magnet arrives and changes nothing

options.text: The domains move freely in air but are locked in the solid, so the iron can never magnetize
options.misconception: confuses domain wall mobility, which is what allows the iron to magnetize at all

questions.explanation: Below its Curie temperature, about 1040 K for iron, a ferromagnet is built from domains inside which the atomic moments are spontaneously aligned. In an unmagnetized sample the domains themselves are oriented at random, so the field of one domain is cancelled by its neighbours and the net magnetization, and with it the external field, is very nearly zero. That is not a weakness but the equilibrium state: a random arrangement has no preference, and a magnet is needed to break the symmetry. Once a magnet is brought near, the field favours domains aligned with it, and the domain walls move so that more domains line up. Their mobility is exactly why soft iron responds easily, which is also why it stays magnetized only while the field is there. The fourth option has this backwards: locking of the walls, not freedom, is what would prevent the iron from responding.
questions.hint: Alignment inside a single domain and alignment of the domains themselves are two different things.

questions.topic: What retentivity measures
questions.learningObjective: define retentivity as the flux density that remains after the field is removed

options.text: The flux density remaining in the bar once the magnetizing field is removed
The flux density the bar reaches when the magnetizing field is made enormous
options.misconception: quotes the saturation value, which is what a very large field gives and not what a coil switched off gives

options.text: The reverse field strength needed to reduce the bar's flux density back to zero
options.misconception: names the coercivity, which is a field strength and would need the coil to be reversed and raised

options.text: The fraction of an applied field that appears as flux inside a closed magnetic circuit
options.misconception: confuses a material property with the flux concentration produced by a particular circuit

questions.explanation: Retentivity is the flux density a magnetized material keeps when the magnetizing field is reduced to zero, and it is what a search coil reads with the magnetizing coil switched off. The corresponding plot is the point where the hysteresis loop crosses the flux density axis, and for a good hard magnet material it is of the order of 1 tesla, so the loop crosses that axis well away from the origin. The first option describes saturation, which is the flux density reached while an enormous field is still being applied and which is not recoverable when the field is removed. The third describes coercivity, and it is measured differently: the magnetizing coil is reversed and its current raised until the bar's flux density falls to zero, so what is read then is a field strength rather than a flux density. The fourth is not a property of the material at all but a property of the circuit built from it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the coil is switched off, reversed, or left at full strength when the reading is taken.

questions.topic: What coercivity measures
questions.learningObjective: define coercivity as the reverse field that reduces the remaining flux to zero
questions.stem: A bar magnet is to be demagnetized. The magnetizing coil is connected to a supply that can be reversed and raised in steps. What quantity is measured as the demagnetization proceeds?

options.text: The flux density remaining after the magnetizing field is switched off
options.misconception: stops at the start of demagnetization, measuring retentivity rather than coercivity

options.text: The largest flux density the material can hold once it is fully magnetized
options.misconception: quotes saturation, which is read while a large field is still applied

options.text: The reverse field strength needed to reduce the remaining flux density to zero
The largest field strength the material can carry with no permanent change whatever
options.misconception: describes a figure of merit combining both loop dimensions rather than the demagnetizing field

questions.explanation: Coercivity is the reverse field strength required to bring the flux density of an already magnetized sample back to zero, so the magnetizing coil is reversed and its current raised until the sample is demagnetized. It is read where the hysteresis loop crosses the flux density axis going the other way, and the value is a field strength in ampere-turns per metre rather than a flux density. The two loop dimensions are therefore complementary: retentivity is a flux density on the vertical axis, coercivity a field strength on the horizontal one, and a material with a large retentivity and a small coercivity is exactly the good permanent magnet, since it keeps its magnetization and resists accidental demagnetization. The first option stops at the start of the procedure, the second is a different measurement entirely, and the fourth is a quality figure rather than something an ammeter in the coil would read.
questions.hint: On the hysteresis loop, one quantity sits on the flux axis and one on the field axis.

questions.topic: Relative permeability from a B and H measurement
questions.learningObjective: obtain a relative permeability from a measured flux density and field strength
questions.stem: A coil around a soft iron core produces a field strength of 100 A per metre in the iron, where the flux density is measured as 1.20 T. Taking mu_0 as 1.3e-6 H per metre, what relative permeability does the material have at that point? Report the number only.

The absolute permeability is B divided by H = 1.20 / 100 = 1.2e-2 H per metre, and the relative permeability is that divided by mu_0, giving 1.2e-2 / 1.3e-6 = 9.231e+3, which is about 9.2e3. Checking forwards, mu_0 mu_r H = 1.3e-6 x 9.231e+3 x 100 = 1.20 T, the measured value. One hygiene point is worth making about the constant. Using the more precise mu_0 of 1.2566e-6 would turn the same measurement into 9.55e3, so the answer should be quoted as 9.2e3 and no further, because the constant supplied has only two significant figures and a three-significant-figure answer built on it would claim precision the data do not carry. A figure of this size is unremarkable: soft iron under working conditions commonly shows relative permeabilities of several thousand, and the figure rises toward its maximum over the region where the material is being magnetized most usefully.
questions.hint: Find the absolute permeability first, then divide by mu_0.

questions.topic: Choosing a core material against choosing a magnet material
questions.learningObjective: match a narrow or wide hysteresis loop to the job the material has to do
questions.stem: Two jobs need opposite properties from an iron-based material: one is a transformer core that must not waste energy, the other a permanent magnet that must keep its magnetization. Which pairing is right?

options.text: A transformer core should be hard steel, because a hard material holds a higher flux density
options.misconception: picks the magnet material for the core, confusing retentivity with the energy lost per cycle

options.text: A permanent magnet should be soft iron, because a soft material holds a larger flux density
options.misconception: picks the core material for the magnet, and soft iron has little retentivity

options.text: Both should be soft iron, since a narrow hysteresis loop loses least energy at any frequency
options.misconception: makes the loop width the only criterion, ignoring that a magnet must not lose its magnetization

options.text: A core wants a narrow loop and low coercivity; a permanent magnet wants a wide loop

questions.explanation: The two jobs pull the loop in opposite directions, and the area of the loop is the energy lost per cycle per unit volume, so a core wants that area as small as possible while a magnet wants its two axis intercepts as large as possible. A core material is therefore chosen for a narrow loop and a small coercive field: a good core might lose 100 joules per cycle per cubic metre, and it will remagnetize to follow the alternating field with little energy. A permanent magnet material is chosen for a broad loop, with a retentivity of order 1 tesla and a coercive field of order 1000 ampere-turns per metre, because what matters is that it resists demagnetization rather than that it economizes on energy. The first two options each assign the wrong material to one of the jobs, and the third assumes a single figure of merit can decide both, which the arithmetic of the loop area shows it cannot.
questions.hint: Ask whether the material is being cycled every half cycle or expected to hold its state.

questions.topic: Energy lost per cycle from a hysteresis loop

questions.stem: The hysteresis loop of a core reaches a flux density of 1.20 T at a field strength of 200 A per metre, and its return branch runs close to a straight line back to the origin, so the loop is approximately a parallelogram. questions.explanation: The area enclosed by the loop is the energy lost per cycle per unit volume, and for a loop shaped as a parallelogram with sides B and H that area is the product of the two extreme values, B H = 1.20 x 200 = 240. The same number follows by splitting the loop into two triangles, each of area one half of B H, which together give B H once more. The figure is a sensible one, sitting at the low end of what published core data give, which is what one expects of a modern alloy at 1.20 T. The tempting wrong answers show two characteristic errors. Halving it to 120 assumes the loop is a triangle rather than a parallelogram, which is right for a material with a small remanence and wrong for one with a large retentivity. Dividing the two quantities instead of multiplying gives 6.0e-3, which has the units of reciprocal permeability rather than energy per volume and is a power of ten away from anything real.
questions.hint: The energy is the area of the loop, so use the two extreme values of the axes it spans.

If the same core were run at 100 Hz the hysteresis figure alone would double to 48 W, and the eddy-current term, treated separately in the next items, would rise faster still.

options.text: It rises in direct proportion, since each cycle sweeps the same area of the loop
It rises with the square of frequency, since each reversal also drives currents in the core
options.misconception: borrows the quadratic scaling that belongs to the eddy-current term, not the loop area

options.text: It rises only with the flux density, because the field reverses more slowly at low frequency
options.misconception: claims no frequency dependence at all, when the area is swept on every cycle whatever

options.misconception: has the sign reversed, though the reason offered about wall speed is the right place to look

Nothing about one sweep depends on how quickly it is made, so the energy per cycle is fixed by the material and the peak flux alone. Multiplying by the number of cycles in a second therefore makes the loss directly proportional to frequency: the 24 W figure becomes 48 W at 100 Hz. questions.topic: How eddy-current loss scales with frequency
questions.learningObjective: state that eddy-current loss goes as the square of frequency and the square of lamination thickness
questions.stem: A core's eddy-current loss is compared at two frequencies and at two lamination thicknesses. Which set of scalings is correct?

options.text: As the square of frequency and as the square of lamination thickness
As the first power of frequency and as the first power of lamination thickness
options.misconception: uses the linear law, which belongs to the hysteresis term swept on each cycle

options.text: As the square of frequency and as the first power of lamination thickness
options.misconception: gets the frequency dependence right but misses that the eddy loops shrink faster than the laminations

options.text: As the first power of frequency and as the square of lamination thickness
options.misconception: pairs the wrong law with the geometry, so neither of the two scalings is right

questions.explanation: The induced current in a lamination is set by the emf across it, and that emf is the flux swing multiplied by the frequency, so the current density in the lamination is proportional to B t f divided by the material's resistivity, where t is the lamination thickness. The power dissipated per unit volume is the resistivity times the square of that current density, so the whole term is proportional to B squared, f squared and t squared, and inversely proportional to the resistivity. Both squares therefore matter and for different reasons: frequency through the emf, thickness through the length of the current loop. The practical consequence is that a core designed for 50 Hz is a poor core at 400 Hz, where the eddy term would be multiplied by 64 while the hysteresis term rose only by 8, so the loss stops being dominated by the loop area and starts being dominated by currents in the iron.

The hysteresis loss is untouched by the change of thickness, so the total core loss falls by less than a factor of four, and beyond some point thinner laminations stop paying, because the cutting cost rises and the interlaminar gaps reduce the effective iron cross-section.

options.misconception: splits the total by an invented rule rather than solving the two equations the data supply

Substitution into the first equation then gives 50a = 40 - 20 = 20, so a = 0.4 and the hysteresis part is 0.4 x 50 = 20 W. Both parts come out positive, and equal shares at the lower frequency are exactly what makes the total triple rather than double when the frequency doubles.

questions.topic: What the Curie temperature marks
questions.learningObjective: state that the Curie temperature is where spontaneous magnetization is lost
questions.stem: A transformer is given a temperature rating. What property of its core material does the rating have to respect, and what is that threshold called?

options.text: The temperature at which the core material's resistance falls to zero
options.misconception: borrows the behaviour of a superconductor, which is not what a core does

options.text: The temperature above which the material loses its spontaneous magnetization
The temperature at which the coil's insulation breaks down and the winding shorts
options.misconception: names an insulation limit, which a good design respects but is not a property of the core

options.text: The temperature at which the field in a core falls to zero for any current whatever
options.misconception: describes a much stronger effect than the gradual loss of ferromagnetism, which is not a transition to zero permeability

questions.explanation: Above the Curie temperature, about 1040 K for iron, the spontaneous alignment of neighbouring atomic moments that makes a ferromagnet magnetic is destroyed by thermal agitation. The material does not become non-magnetic: it becomes paramagnetic, with a relative permeability of order 1, so it behaves much as air would in the same circuit and the magnetizing current rises steeply. That is the physical reason a transformer's rating is quoted in degrees, since crossing the threshold would take the core out of service long before its insulation failed. questions.explanation: Faraday's law puts a rate of change inside the expression, and the rate here is zero. Move the block, and the flux through a given loop changes; change the field, and so does the flux; and screen part of the field out with a nearby iron piece, which again changes it. Each of those produces an emf, and the block's resistance then converts the resulting current into heat, which is the whole basis of eddy-current heating and of eddy-current braking. The third option describes a Hall voltage, which requires charge already flowing through the block and has nothing to do with the applied field alone.

options.misconception: describes a connection that would short the rotor and stop it starting at all

A practical consequence is the persistent-current ring: a ring cooled with flux through it and then left alone keeps that flux indefinitely, since the zero resistance gives the induced current no reason to decay. The second option is the behaviour of a perfect conductor, which traps whatever flux existed at the moment its resistance vanished and shows no expulsion at all, and the other two describe changes in the wrong direction or in the wrong place.

options.misconception: makes the two parts one current either side of a temperature, not two simultaneous parts

options.text: One flowing in the material and one confined to the surface screening layer
options.misconception: divides the current between bulk and surface, which is a different division altogether

options.text: A normal part that is squeezed out on cooling and a superfluid part that carries no resistance

questions.explanation: Just above the critical temperature all the carriers are normal, and each is slowed by scattering. As the temperature falls the fraction in a condensate grows, and the condensate part accelerates without scattering and so contributes no resistance; the model calls the remainder a normal fluid that is being progressively squeezed out. At 4.2 K a typical niobium-titanium conductor has roughly half its carriers in the superfluid state, so the two parts are of comparable size rather than one being negligible. The model earns its place because the two parts respond differently in time. The superfluid part follows a changing field immediately, while the normal part lags, so a superconductor shows a small frequency-dependent loss that falls to nothing as the frequency falls, instead of being simply perfect at all times. That is why the zero-resistance statement is exact only in the direct-current limit.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the fraction of carriers that scatter as the temperature falls.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why a superconductor can hold a magnet up
questions.learningObjective: explain levitation by persistent screening currents in a superconductor
questions.stem: A small permanent magnet rests above the surface of a type-II superconductor with nothing holding it up. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The magnet is repelled because the superconductor has itself become permanently magnetized
options.misconception: credits the superconductor with a permanent moment, which it does not develop

options.text: The magnet is supported because the induced current in the superconductor has a resistance
options.misconception: requires a resistance, and a resistive current would decay and the support would vanish

options.text: Induced currents oppose the magnet's approach, and zero resistance keeps them flowing
The magnet is held up by the pressure of the cold helium gas trapped underneath it
options.misconception: invents a mechanical support from the cryogen, which plays no part in the force

questions.explanation: The force is magnetic, and its direction is fixed by Lenz's law. As the magnet approaches, the flux through the superconductor increases, the induced currents flow so as to oppose that increase, and the magnet is pushed away. Because the resistance is zero those currents do not decay, so the repelling field persists indefinitely rather than fading as it would in a piece of copper. With the magnet held still, the superconductor is a picture of the trapped-flux state discussed earlier, and the same currents are what keep the field from entering the material at all. Flux pinning in a type-II superconductor adds a second contribution, for the flux lines threaded through it are held against movement, and that is what makes the hover stable rather than merely repulsive. A gram of magnet is held by a force of order 0.01 N, and a few hundred grams is within reach at 4.2 K. The second option would be correct for a piece of copper only in the first instant of the approach.
questions.hint: Ask what the induced current is doing, and what would happen to it if the resistance were not zero.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Hall voltage in a doped semiconductor
questions.learningObjective: compute the Hall voltage of a rectangular slab from current, field, thickness and density
questions.stem: A rectangular semiconductor slab is 5.00 mm wide and 0.500 mm thick, and carries a current of 0.250 A along its length. A field of 0.400 T is applied perpendicular to the broad face, and the carrier density is 8.50e22 per cubic metre. Taking e as 1.602e-19 C, what is the Hall voltage across the width, in volts? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The Hall voltage is the current times the field divided by the carrier density, the charge and the thickness, so it is 0.250 x 0.400 divided by (8.50e22 x 1.602e-19 x 5.00e-4), and the denominator is 6.81, giving 1.469e-2 V, that is 14.7 millivolts. Working through the physics rather than the formula gives the same figure and is worth the detour, because it shows which dimension does what. The current density is 0.250 divided by (5.00e-3 x 5.00e-4) = 1.00e5 A per square metre, the drift speed follows as 1.00e5 divided by the number density times the charge, which is 7.34 m per second, and the Hall field across the slab is that speed times the applied field, 2.94 V per metre. Multiplied by the 5.00 mm width, the width is what the voltage is measured across, and that gives 14.7 millivolts once more. The 14.7 millivolt figure is a sensible working value for a doped semiconductor, where carriers are sparse enough for the effect to be measurable at all.
questions.hint: Find the drift speed of the carriers first, then the field they produce across the width.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Carrier density from a Hall measurement
questions.learningObjective: recover a carrier density from a Hall voltage, current, field and thickness
questions.stem: A slab 1.00 mm thick carries a current of 0.400 A with a magnetic field of 0.250 T across it, and the Hall voltage measured across the slab is 5.00 mV. Taking e as 1.602e-19 C, what is the carrier density, in carriers per cubic metre? Report the number only.

options.text: 5.00e-5 per cubic metre, which is the Hall coefficient rather than a density
options.misconception: quotes the Hall coefficient in the slot where a carrier density belongs

options.text: 1.25e23 per cubic metre, from the charge times the Hall coefficient inverted
1.25e24 per cubic metre, from reading the thickness as 0.100 mm rather than 1.00 mm
options.misconception: misreads the thickness by a factor of ten, which the density inherits in reverse

options.text: 6.24e22 per cubic metre, from charging the carriers as pairs rather than singly
options.misconception: treats every carrier as a pair with twice the charge, which halves the answer

questions.explanation: The Hall coefficient is the Hall voltage times the thickness divided by the current and the field, so it is 5.00e-3 x 1.00e-3 divided by 0.400 x 0.250, which is 5.00e-5 cubic metres per coulomb, and the carrier density is one over the charge times that coefficient, 1 / (1.602e-19 x 5.00e-5) = 1.248e+23 per cubic metre. Substituting everything in one line gives the same result, since the current times the field divided by the charge, the thickness and the Hall voltage is 0.400 x 0.250 divided by (1.602e-19 x 1.00e-3 x 5.00e-3) = 0.100 divided by 8.01e-25, again 1.248e+23. The plausibility check is the important one: 1.2e23 per cubic metre is 1.2e17 per cubic centimetre, a light doping of a semiconductor, and it sits comfortably above the roughly 1e19 per cubic centimetre at which carriers begin to pair up as in a superconductor. That is the trap in the fourth option, which halves the answer by charging every carrier as a pair.
questions.hint: Form the Hall coefficient from the reading and the geometry, then invert it with the charge.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Reading carrier type from the sign of a Hall voltage
questions.learningObjective: use the sign of a Hall voltage to identify whether electrons or holes carry the current
questions.stem: A slab is measured in the same apparatus, with the current and the field kept in the same directions as before, and the Hall voltage now has the opposite sign. What does the changed sign indicate?

options.text: The dominant carriers are now holes rather than electrons, since the two drift in opposite senses
The temperature has changed, since the sign of a Hall reading is set by the mobility
options.misconception: confuses the size of a reading with its sign, which mobility cannot change

options.text: The field has been reversed, which flips the direction of the Hall field by Lenz's law
options.misconception: invents a change that the conditions of the measurement exclude

options.text: The contacts have been swapped over, which reverses the reading without changing anything else
options.misconception: offers a wiring fault as the cause, where a genuine change in the sample is meant

questions.explanation: The Hall coefficient is inversely proportional to the carrier charge, so it carries a sign: electrons are negative and holes are positive, and the Hall voltage inherits that sign in a fixed arrangement of current, field and contacts. In the laboratory the same thing is achieved by annealing, since a material can be driven from one type of carrier to the other by changing its doping or its stoichiometry, and once the majority carrier has changed the sign of the reading changes permanently. That is what makes the sign useful rather than decorative: it is how the type is identified without having to model the band structure. The third option would be a genuine effect if it had happened, since reversing the field does reverse the reading, but the measurement as specified keeps the field fixed. The fourth is a useful thing to check on a bench, but it is a fault rather than a change in the physics of the sample.
questions.hint: The Hall coefficient is inversely proportional to the carrier charge, and charges of opposite sign are what matter.

questions.topic: Carrier mobility from drift speed and driving field
questions.learningObjective: obtain a carrier mobility from a drift speed and the field driving it
questions.stem: The carriers in the slab just described drift at 7.34 m per second when a driving field of 2.50 V per metre is applied across them. What is their mobility, in square metres per volt second? Report the number only.

options.text: 0.340, from dividing the driving field by the drift speed rather than the reverse
options.misconception: inverts the ratio, which is the commonest slip when the units are not written out

options.text: 18.4, from multiplying the drift speed by the driving field instead of dividing
options.misconception: multiplies the two inputs instead of forming a ratio between them

options.text: 2.94, from the drift speed divided by the driving field
2.50, from reading off the driving field and ignoring the drift speed entirely
options.misconception: quotes one of the two inputs and ignores the other altogether

questions.explanation: Mobility is the drift speed per unit driving field, so 7.34 divided by 2.50 is 2.94 square metres per volt second, which is 2.9e4 square centimetres per volt second in the units usually quoted for semiconductors. A second route ties it to the Hall result. With a carrier density of 8.50e22 and a charge of 1.602e-19 the number density times the charge is 1.36e4 per cubic metre per coulomb, and the conductivity is that product times the mobility, 1.36e4 x 2.94 = 4.00e4 S per metre, so the resistivity is 2.50e-5 ohm metres. Those are the right numbers for a lightly doped semiconductor, and the mobility sits well above the 1e-2 square metres per volt second typical of a metal, because a metal's carriers are far more numerous and so each has less room to accelerate. The first option inverts the ratio and the second multiplies, both of which are easy slips when the units of the inputs are not written down first.
questions.hint: Mobility is a drift speed divided by the field that produces the drift.

questions.topic: Why a metal gives a tiny Hall voltage
questions.learningObjective: explain that a metal's very large carrier density makes its Hall voltage very small
questions.stem: Copper and the semiconductor just discussed are cut into identical Hall plates and measured at the same current and field. What is expected, and why?

options.text: The copper gives a large Hall voltage, because a metal carries far more current in total
options.misconception: confuses the total current, which is held fixed, with the carrier density inside the voltage expression

options.text: The copper gives a much smaller voltage, because it has vastly more carriers sharing it
Both give the same voltage, because the Hall expression does not mention the density
options.misconception: denies the density term, which is the one place the two materials differ most

options.text: The copper gives no voltage at all, because a metal has no mobile charge carriers
options.misconception: removes the carriers entirely, when a metal is the best conductor known

questions.explanation: The Hall voltage is the current times the field divided by the carrier density, the charge and the thickness, and the carrier density is where the two materials diverge. Copper carries about 8.5e28 carriers per cubic metre against the 8.5e22 of the slab, a ratio of a million, so with everything else matched the copper's Hall voltage is a million times smaller. Taking the 14.7 millivolts of the semiconductor, the copper figure is 1.5e-8 V, which is why Hall plates cut from metals need amplifiers of enormous gain and are used chiefly as magnetic field probes rather than as a measurement of carrier density. The third option is the one most often assumed and is easily disproved: the expression for the Hall voltage contains the density explicitly. The fourth is a straightforward confusion, since a metal is the best conductor available precisely because it has the most mobile carriers.
questions.hint: Look at which factor differs most between a metal and a doped semiconductor.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Cyclotron frequency of a charged particle
questions.learningObjective: compute the cyclotron frequency of a particle from its charge, mass and field
questions.stem: An electron moves in a uniform magnetic field of 0.500 T. Taking e as 1.602e-19 C and the electron mass as 9.109e-31 kg, what is the cyclotron frequency, the rate at which it turns, in hertz? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The magnetic force turns the electron in a circle, and equating that to the required centripetal force gives an angular rate of e B over m, which is 1.602e-19 x 0.500 / 9.109e-31 = 8.794e+10 per second. The frequency in hertz is that divided by 2 pi, giving 1.3995e+10 Hz, that is 14.0 GHz. Working from the period instead is the same statement in a different order: the time for one circle is 2 pi m over e B = 7.15e-11 s, and the reciprocal of that is 1.3995e+10 Hz. Plausibility has two anchors. The rate per tesla comes out at 2.799e+10 Hz per tesla, so 0.500 T giving 14 GHz is the expected figure, and a proton in the same field circles at only 7.620e+6 Hz, some two thousand times more slowly, because the ratio depends on charge over mass and the proton is 1836 times heavier.
questions.hint: Equate the magnetic force to the centripetal force, then divide the angular rate by 2 pi.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Precession frequency of a nucleus in a field
questions.learningObjective: compute a nuclear precession frequency from the gyromagnetic ratio and the field
questions.stem: A specimen is placed in the field of a 2.35 T magnet. The nucleus under study has a gyromagnetic ratio of 42.58 MHz per tesla. What precession frequency does it show, in hertz? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: A magnetic moment in a field does not point along it but precesses about it at a rate set by the gyromagnetic ratio, and the frequency form of that ratio is quoted in megahertz per tesla, so the answer is 42.58e6 multiplied by 2.35, which is 1.0006e+8 Hz, that is 100.1 MHz. The angular form gives the same figure by a different route: with a ratio of 2 pi times 42.58e6, or 2.675e8 per second per tesla, the angular rate is 2.675e8 x 2.35 = 6.286e8 per second, and dividing by 2 pi returns 1.0006e+8 Hz. The plausibility check is that a magnet of 2.35 T gives protons a frequency of about 100 MHz, which is the standard commercial NMR frequency, chosen because the wavelength of radio waves at that frequency gives convenient equipment. The linear dependence on the field is also a practical lever: doubling the field doubles every resonance in the spectrum and spreads the chemical shifts out, which is why high-field machines are worth their cost.
questions.hint: Multiply the quoted frequency form of the gyromagnetic ratio by the field.

questions.topic: Electron spin resonance frequency
questions.learningObjective: compute a spin resonance frequency from the g factor, Bohr magneton and field
questions.stem: An unpaired electron of g factor 2.002 is in a magnetic field of 0.335 T. Taking the Bohr magneton as 9.274e-24 J per tesla and h as 6.626e-34 J s, what resonance frequency does it show, in hertz? Report the number only.

options.text: 4.69e9 Hz, from leaving the g factor out of the energy gap
options.misconception: drops the g factor, a tempting slip because its value is so close to 2

options.text: 1.88e10 Hz, from applying the factor of two in the g factor twice over
options.misconception: counts the factor of two in the g value a second time as well

options.text: 5.90e10 Hz, from dividing the energy gap by the reduced Planck constant
options.misconception: divides by the reduced constant, which gives the angular rate rather than the frequency

options.text: 9.39e9 Hz, from the energy gap divided by the Planck constant

A second route avoids the energy gap altogether: the Bohr magneton divided by the Planck constant is 1.3996e10 Hz per tesla, and multiplying that by the g factor and the field gives 1.3996e10 x 2.002 x 0.335, again 9.3870e+9 Hz. The plausibility check is that about 9.4 GHz at 0.335 T is the X band used in benchtop spectrometers, where 0.34 T is the standard magnet field. The third option divides by the reduced Planck constant, which yields the angular rate of 5.90e10 per second, exactly 2 pi times the frequency; the first drops the g factor, which is the classic error because the value is so close to 2 that it is tempting to ignore.
questions.hint: Find the energy gap between the two states, then divide it by the Planck constant.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why different nuclei resonate at different rates
questions.learningObjective: explain that nuclei differ in precession rate through their gyromagnetic ratios
questions.stem: Two different nuclei are put in the same 2.35 T magnet in the same sample. Why do they resonate at different frequencies rather than at the same one?

options.text: Their gyromagnetic ratios differ, so the same field spins each of them at its own rate
Their charges differ, so each nucleus feels a different magnetic force in the same field
options.misconception: makes the charge alone responsible, whereas the rate depends on a ratio of two quantities

options.text: Their masses differ, so the heavier one is slowed by its inertia with its moment unchanged
options.misconception: treats the magnetic moment as fixed while the mass changes, which is not how the ratio behaves

options.text: Their moments differ in proportion to their masses, so the two ratios come out equal
options.misconception: makes the ratio mass-invariant, which would make the two nuclei indistinguishable

questions.explanation: The precession rate is the ratio of the nuclear magnetic moment to its angular momentum, packaged as the gyromagnetic ratio, and that ratio is different for every nucleus. Protons have a ratio of 42.58 MHz per tesla, so in a 2.35 T magnet they give the 100.1 MHz worked out above, while carbon 13 has a ratio of about 10.7 MHz per tesla and therefore appears at 25.1 MHz in the same field. The two are then separated by tens of megahertz in one spectrum, which is what lets a spectrometer distinguish them. Mass does enter the ratio, so the third option is not far from the truth in spirit, but the magnetic moment does not stay fixed while the mass changes, and the fourth option, which claims the ratio is mass-invariant, is contradicted by the two numbers just quoted. Charge alone, as the second option has it, is not what is measured. A further few parts per million separates nuclei of the same element in different chemical environments, and that small chemical shift is what makes the technique a structural tool.
questions.hint: The rate is a ratio of the magnetic moment to the angular momentum, and that ratio is nucleus specific.
